phonemes.desc: The onset cluster [mj], m followed by a palatal glide, as in English 'music'; the anglicized Mjolnir keeps the spelling but usually drops the glide
Short open-mid back rounded [ɔ], written o-ogonek; the rounded 'o' of 'hot', held short — distinct from both o and ó
Long or geminated alveolar lateral [lː], written double in Old Norse to show length; hold it like the ll of Italian 'bella'

pronunciation.approximation: 'MYAWL-lnir' — begin with the mj of 'music', sound the vowel like the short rounded 'o' of 'hot', and hold the ll double before the final '-nir'.

pronunciation.note: Mjǫllnir is Tier 1: the o-ogonek ǫ (the short rounded [ɔ] of Old Norse) and the geminate ll are features the ASCII form loses — this is the normalized dictionary form (Cleasby–Vigfusson, s.v. 'Mjöllnir'; Zoëga, s.v. 'Mjǫllnir'), with the living Icelandic Mjölnir as the attested modern variant. The etymology is genuinely disputed: proposals connect the name to Old Norse mala, 'to grind' ('the grinder'), to mjǫll, 'new snow' ('the shining one'), and to the Slavic lightning word seen in Russian mólnija, and the scholarship has settled on none of them.

domains.title: Thunder, Hallowing, Return
domains.subtitle: The domain of Mjǫllnir
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Mjǫllnir is the hammer of Þórr — the one treasure the gods cannot do without. Dwarf-forged and short in the haft from Loki's sabotage, it never misses its mark, never flies so far that it fails to return to the thrower's hand, and shrinks small enough to be hidden inside a shirt. With it Þórr holds the wall between Ásgarðr and the giants.

Yet the hammer is not only a weapon. It is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage, raised over the newborn, and lifted against the dead man's pyre — it blessed Baldr's burning ship. In the Viking Age men and women wore it in silver and iron around their necks, the heathen answer to the Christian cross, and it is worn again today.

cards.name: The Dwarven Forge
cards.desc: Wagered into being by Loki, forged by the dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr; a fly's bite at the bellows left the haft too short.

cards.name: The Stolen Hammer
cards.desc: Þrymr the giant buried it eight miles down and demanded Freyja as bride-price; Þórr won it back veiled as the bride.

cards.name: Hammer of Hallowing
cards.desc: The same weapon that shatters giants consecrates brides, newborns, and funeral pyres — destruction and blessing in one tool.

cards.name: The Worn Hammer
cards.desc: Viking-age smiths cast it by the hundred in silver and iron; the pendant answered the cross then and signifies heathen faith now.

symbols.name: The short haft
symbols.meaning: The flaw left by Loki's fly-form sabotage at the bellows — the defect that makes the hammer a one-handed weapon

symbols.name: The unerring throw
symbols.meaning: It never misses its target and never flies so far that it fails to return to the thrower's hand

symbols.name: The hidden hammer
symbols.meaning: It shrinks small enough to be kept inside the shirt — power carried unseen

symbols.name: Lightning made iron
symbols.meaning: The thunderbolt given haft and head, the storm wielded as a tool

symbols.name: The amulet
symbols.meaning: The pendant form worn across the Viking world, the heathen counterpart of the cross

mythology.lead: Mjǫllnir is the most famous weapon in the northern world and the busiest: no other treasure of the gods both kills and consecrates. Forged as the stake in one of Loki's wagers, it came out of Sindri's forge with a haft too short — and the gods judged it the best of all treasures anyway. The sources hand it four great stories: its flawed making, its theft, its duel, and its blessing of the dead god's pyre.

myths.title: The Wager and the Short Haft
myths.text:
After Loki shears Sif's hair, he must replace it, and from the sons of Ívaldi he commissions hair of living gold, the ship Skíðblaðnir, and the spear Gungnir. Swaggering, he wagers his head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three finer treasures. At the forge, Loki becomes a fly and bites Brokkr at the bellows — arm, then neck, and Brokkr does not falter; but the third bite lands on his eyelid, and blinded by his own blood for one stroke of the bellows, he mars the work. Out of the forge comes a hammer — with a haft too short (Skáldskaparmál, trans. Brodeur).

Brokkr names its virtues to Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr: swung, it never fails; thrown, it never misses; it returns to the hand of its own will; and it shrinks small enough to be kept inside the shirt. Only the short haft is held against it — and the gods judge it the best of all six treasures, 'for with it Þórr can defend us against the mountain-giants.' Loki, defeated by the very sabotage he taught, keeps his head only by a trick. The myth means the flaw in the gods' most trusted tool is the permanent signature of the adversary's interference.

myths.title: The Hammer in the Bride's Lap
myths.text:
Þórr wakes one morning and the hammer is gone. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Jötunheimr, and hears Þrymr boast that he has buried Mjǫllnir eight leagues down — and that no one recovers it unless Freyja is brought to him as bride. Freyja's refusal shakes her hall and snaps the necklace Brísingamen, so Heimdallr proposes the unthinkable: dress Þórr as the bride. The thunder-god protests — until Loki answers that without the hammer the giants will soon hold Ásgarðr. Veiled, hung with Brísingamen and jingling keys, Þórr rides east with Loki as his maidservant (Þrymskviða).

The comedy is exact: the 'bride' devours an ox and eight salmon and drains three casks of mead, while Loki explains to the startled groom that Freyja has eaten nothing and slept not at all for longing. Þrymr lifts the veil for a kiss and leaps the hall's length from the fire in her eyes. Then he calls for the hammer — to hallow the bride, laid on her knees by the hand of Vár — and Þórr's heart laughs in his breast. His hand closes on the haft; he kills Þrymr, then the giant's whole household. The joke has a hard core: the hammer laid in the bride's lap is not a stage prop but the consecration itself — and the mightiest of the Æsir must wear bridal linen to recover his own.

myths.title: Hrungnir and the Whetstone
myths.text: The hammer's most dangerous duel came against the giant Hrungnir, who boasted in Asgard itself that he would kill all the gods, carry Freyja and Sif off to Jötunheimr, and drain the Æsir's ale. The gods sent for Þórr, and at the ford of Grjótúnagarðar the giant waited behind his stone shield, hurling his whetstone weapon. Mjǫllnir and the whetstone met in mid-air: the hammer smashed the stone and drove on into Hrungnir's skull — but a shard of whetstone lodged in Þórr's own head. The god walked home with the fragment still in him, and the sorceress Gróa was summoned to sing it loose. Her spells worked; Þórr felt it stir, and in his joy told her that her long-lost husband was on his way home — Gróa forgot her charms mid-verse in her delight, and the whetstone stayed in Þórr's skull forever. Snorri adds the custom: whetstones are forbidden as grave-goods, for this reason. The myth means the hammer's victories are never clean — its greatest triumph left its bearer permanently scarred, and the one thing Mjǫllnir could not fix was the wound it won by.

myths.title: Hallowing Baldr's Pyre
myths.text: When Baldr lies dead, the gods build his pyre on the ship Hringhorni, and the giantess Hyrrokkin, riding a wolf with vipers for reins, must be fetched to launch it. Baldr's wife Nanna dies of grief and is laid beside him. Þórr steps forward and hallows the pyre with Mjǫllnir — the god of thunder blessing the burning of the best of the gods — and when a dwarf named Litr runs across his path, he kicks him into the flames (Gylfaginning). The same gesture revives his slaughtered goats after they have been eaten, hallows the bride at the wedding feast, and here blesses the grave. Hammer at the cradle, hammer at the marriage-bed, hammer at the pyre: Snorri's picture of Þórr is of a god whose weapon marks every threshold of life — destruction and consecration in one motion, never separated. The Viking-age custom of wearing the hammer at the throat simply hung that threshold-power around the neck.

lore.syncretism:
The hammer did not stay inside Iceland's manuscripts. On the continent its god appears as Donar, and when Adam of Bremen describes the temple at Uppsala he says that Thor 'with his mace looks like Jupiter' — the interpretatio romana equating thunder with thunder. Saxo Grammaticus gives Thor an oak club and, tellingly, preserves the short handle: in the Gesta Danorum the hero Høther disables the weapon by lopping off its shaft, an euhemerized echo of the fly at the bellows. Archaeology reaches further back: scholars have long connected the hammer pendants to the older club-of-Hercules amulets of the Roman frontier provinces, and Bronze Age rock carvings already show axe- and hammer-bearing figures in consecrating poses.

Comparativists place Mjǫllnir in a wide Indo-European family of thunder-weapons — Indra's vajra, the club of the Dagda, the axe of Perun — and one proposed etymology would make the name itself a cousin of Slavic mólnija, 'lightning', though the derivation is contested. In later folklore the weapon survived transmuted: Neolithic axe-heads and belemnites were kept as 'thunder-stones' (torshammare), guards against lightning, and early-modern Icelandic grimoires went so far as to label the swastika 'Thor's hammer'. The twentieth century folded the hammer back into myth again through comics and film — a modern transmutation as thorough as any Saxo performed.
lore.culturalLegacy: Nineteenth-century art made the hammer visible: Mårten Eskil Winge's Thor's Fight with the Giants (1872) swings it over the goat-chariot, and the book illustrations of Lorenz Frølich and Elmer Boyd Smith fixed the bridal veil and the forge in the popular imagination. In Wagner's Ring it is Donner — the continental Þórr — who raises the hammer in Das Rheingold to summon the storm that clears the air for the rainbow bridge to Valhalla. Games have made the weapon interactive, from Smite and Valheim to God of War Ragnarök, where Mjölnir is an antagonist's instrument. Marvel's Mjolnir, introduced in 1962, added the 'worthiness' enchantment — whosoever holds this hammer — a modern invention with no Eddic basis, and arguably the single most successful addition to the mythology since Snorri. In modern Heathenry and Ásatrú the hammer is worn and wielded again in earnest: the hamarsigna, the sign of the hammer, blesses rites much as the sources describe, and since 2013 the Mjölnir emblem has been approved for the government headstones of American service members. Restoring Mjǫllnir in Unicode preserves the name's Old Norse specificity — the rounded ǫ and the geminate ll — against the flattening force of plain ASCII.
lore.extendedMeditation: The hammer is the argument that the fiercest weapon is also the holiest instrument — that the force which breaks the giants is the same force that blesses the bride, the child, and the dead. Its haft is short because perfection was sabotaged and the flaw endured; gods and men alike made do with the tool they had, and it was enough. For a thousand years people wore this name against their skin as the storm made portable, protection you could carry. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form.

lore.archaeology: The hammer is one of the best-attested symbols of the Viking age. Around a thousand Mjǫllnir pendants in iron, silver, and amber have been unearthed across Scandinavia, England, northern Germany, the Baltic, and Russia — most simply made, about a hundred with ornament, and a tenth from graves, predominantly women's cremations; Jörn Staecker's typology (1999) and Katherine Beard's Eitri database (2019) order the material. Famous finds include the Rømersdal hammer from Bornholm, the gold-plated Bredsätra pendant from Öland, the Foss 'wolf-cross' from Iceland that reads as cross and hammer at once, and the Hiddensee gold treasure, where a hammer hangs among crosses. The Købelev hammer from Lolland (10th century) is the only one that names itself, inscribed in Younger Futhark 'hamar × is' — 'this is a hammer' — and the 11th-century Kvinneby copper amulet from Öland invokes Þórr's protection 'with his hammer' in runes. Thor's hammer is carved on runestones (DR 26, DR 48, DR 120, VG 113, Sö 86, Sö 111) and appears in the fishing scenes on the Altuna stone and at Gosforth; the small bronze Eyrarland figure from Iceland (c. AD 1000) may show the god gripping it. Textually, Þrymskviða and Lokasenna survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), the forging and the hallowing of Baldr's pyre in the Prose Edda manuscripts, above all the Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is Mjǫllnir, with o-ogonek for the short rounded vowel [ɔ] and a geminate ll; the medieval manuscripts wrote it in Latin letters, varying between miǫllnir, miöllnir, and kindred spellings. In the Viking age itself the word was carved, not written: the Younger Futhark, the sixteen-rune alphabet of the period, carries both of the hammer's surviving runic witnesses — the Købelev amulet's proud hamar × is ('this is a hammer') and the Kvinneby amulet's invocation of Þórr 'with his hammer'. The site's Unicode restoration Mjǫllnir keeps what ASCII cannot: the o-ogonek and the geminate ll of the dictionary form, registrable as the internationalized domain mjǫllnir.com (punycode xn--mjllnir-bnc.com). The plain form mjolnir survives only as the anglicized shadow — the name as comics rendered it, with the old rounded vowel and the long lateral filed away.
